voiceover.text: Here's the table, with its third column still empty. A marathon runner who's trained well and paced well can still slow dramatically at around thirty-two kilometres. Runners call it hitting the wall. But that runner is carrying enough fat to run several more marathons. So what's actually run out? And second, after a hundred-metre sprint, you keep breathing hard for minutes. So what's all that oxygen for?

The third system is the aerobic system. It finishes the job glycolysis starts. Instead of stopping early, it breaks fuel all the way down, inside the mitochondria, using oxygen, and leaves only carbon dioxide and water. Fill the column. Fuel: carbohydrate and fat, with a little protein. Efficiency: more than thirty ATP per glucose, against two without oxygen. So it's by far the most productive system, and the slowest. Duration: it leads from about two minutes, and can run for hours. Intensity: low to moderate, up to about eighty-five per cent of maximum effort. Recovery: slow, up to two days to refill glycogen, and days to repair tissue. And fatigue: glycogen runs low, fluid runs low, the body overheats, and the brain's drive falls. Nothing builds up to poison the muscle.

Why so slow? Phosphocreatine and glucose are already in the fibre. Oxygen isn't. It has to be breathed in, loaded onto haemoglobin, pumped by the heart, and diffused into the muscle before one aerobic ATP is made. So this system can never be faster than the delivery chain that feeds it. That's what caps its intensity. And it's why aerobic fatigue is a supply problem. Marathon runners plan their fuel, fluids and pace. Sprinters don't need to.

So which fuel does it burn? Fat holds more than twice the energy per gram, and even a lean athlete stores enough for many hours. Carbohydrate is a small store, about ninety minutes to two hours of hard work. But fat releases its energy slowly, and needs more oxygen for each unit of energy. Carbohydrate is faster, and it's the only food fuel the body can use without oxygen. So intensity decides the mix. At rest and at low intensity, fat leads. As the pace rises, the body shifts toward carbohydrate, because fat can't be supplied fast enough. Fat is the bigger tank, but the narrower pipe.

Now the marathon. By around thirty-two kilometres, muscle and liver glycogen are nearly gone. Plenty of fat is left, but fat alone can't be released fast enough to hold race pace. So the runner doesn't stop. The pace drops to one that fat can supply, and that sudden drop is the wall. They haven't run out of energy. They've run out of the fuel that's fast enough. That's why endurance athletes load up on carbohydrate beforehand, and eat it during events longer than about ninety minutes.

The aerobic system's slow start causes a problem at both ends of a session. When you start running, demand jumps at once, but heart rate, stroke volume and breathing take a minute or two to catch up. That gap is the oxygen deficit, and the anaerobic systems cover it. It's why the first minutes of a run feel harder, and why a warm-up helps: it raises supply before the real work starts. Once supply meets demand, you're in a steady state, and you can keep going. Push above what oxygen can cover, and there's no steady state. The effort now has a time limit.

At the other end, you stop, but your oxygen use stays high. That's excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, or EPOC. The extra oxygen pays for recovery. It rebuilds phosphocreatine and ATP, clears the lactate, and reloads oxygen onto haemoglobin and onto myoglobin, the muscle's own oxygen store. So recovery isn't doing nothing. It costs energy. That's why a light cool-down clears by-products faster than sitting down.

Now the part of the dot point most answers leave out: interplay. All three systems run all the time. What changes is the share each one supplies, and intensity and duration set those shares, moment by moment. Take a netball match. Every sprint, jump and change of direction is mostly ATP-PCr. A long passage of hard defence pushes glycolysis up. But most of a sixty-minute match is walking and jogging, so across the whole match, the aerobic system supplies most of the energy.

So why should a netballer train aerobically, when no single effort lasts more than a few seconds? Because the aerobic system is what recovers them between efforts. In every walk and jog, it rebuilds phosphocreatine and clears by-products. A fitter player rebuilds faster, so they reach the next sprint with more fast fuel. That doesn't show up as a faster single sprint. It shows up in the last quarter, as sprints that stay sharp. Aerobic fitness in team sport is about the recovery, not the running.
Two things to remember. Fat is the bigger tank, but the narrower pipe. And in team sport, aerobic fitness is about the recovery, not the running.

Two exam questions. First. A coach tells a half-marathon runner to go out hard and bank time while they're fresh. Explain why this is likely to slow their finish, referring to fuel use. Pause here to answer.

A faster start raises intensity, so a bigger share of the energy comes from carbohydrate. That empties the small glycogen store sooner. Once it's low, the pace falls to what fat can supply, late and suddenly. The classic mistake is saying the runner simply runs out of energy.
Second. Analyse the interplay of the energy systems across a fifteen-hundred-metre race, from the start to the final sprint. Pause here to answer.

All three systems run throughout. The fast start is mostly ATP-PCr. Glycolysis rises, then eases as the aerobic system reaches a steady state and supplies most of the middle. In the final sprint, glycolysis rises sharply again. Over a race of about four minutes, aerobic supplies the most. The classic mistake is a relay: one system, then the next.

So, for any activity, name all three systems, then say what sets their shares. But every system needs its fuel, and the wall showed that the wrong fuel at the wrong time ends a race. So what should an athlete eat?
